message.content:
Below is a concise summary of key tenant‑rights protections you enjoy when renting property in Texas. These points reflect current statutes and common‑law principles; they do **not** constitute formal legal advice—if your situation involves disputes, eviction notices, or other complex issues, consult a licensed attorney or a qualified tenant‑advocacy organization. | Category | Typical Rights & Protections | |----------|------------------------------| | **Security Deposit Limits** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent if the lease term ≤ 12 months.
• For leases > 12 months, the limit rises to two months’ rent.
• Deposits must be returned within 30 days after tenancy ends unless deductions are justified. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Property must meet basic health and safety standards (adequate heating/air conditioning, plumbing, electrical wiring, structural integrity).
• If major repairs aren’t made promptly, tenants may have remedies such as withholding rent, repairing themselves and deducting costs, or terminating the lease. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Tenants may occupy premises without unreasonable interference from landlords or others acting on landlord’s behalf. | | **Notice Requirements** | • Eviction requires at least 90 days’ written notice for nonpayment of rent.
• Other reasons for termination typically require 30–60 day notice depending on lease terms. | | **Discrimination Protection** | • Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Civil Rights Code, discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, source of income, marital status, age, sexual orientation, gender identity, or veteran status is prohibited. | | **Lease Terms & Modifications** | • Written agreements govern most aspects of tenancy. Oral modifications are generally enforceable only if both parties agree. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory cap on increases except where governed by a “rent control” ordinance (rare in Texas). However, landlords must still follow proper notice procedures. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Lease usually governs whether subleasing is allowed; many leases prohibit it without consent. | | **Landlord Access** | • Landlords must provide reasonable notice (typically 24 hours) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | ### Practical Steps for Protecting Your Tenant Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – All obligations and restrictions are spelled out there. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, repair requests, and photos of conditions. 3. **Know When to File a Complaint** – Contact the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR), local consumer protection office, or the Texas Attorney General’s Office if you suspect unlawful practices. 4. **Seek Mediation First** – Many cities offer free mediation services between landlords and tenants. ### Helpful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |---------|---------------| | [Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/) | Guides on rental laws, how to file complaints, and tenant rights brochures. | | [Tennessee Housing Finance Agency (THFA)](http://thfa.org/) | Not directly applicable, but offers educational materials on fair housing. | | Local County Clerk’s Office | Records of evictions filed against landlords. | | Legal Aid Organizations (e.g., Texas RioGrande Legal Aid, Lone Star Legal Services) | Free or low‑cost representation for qualifying tenants. | | National Apartment Association (NAA) – *Tenant Handbook* | State‑by‑state breakdowns of tenant rights. | --- #### Quick Checklist Before Signing Anything - Verify the landlord has complied with the required disclosure statements (security deposit receipt, lead paint disclosures if applicable). - Confirm the lease length matches what was promised verbally. - Ensure the lease includes clear clauses on maintenance responsibilities and dispute resolution mechanisms. If you’re facing immediate problems—such as being threatened with eviction, having essential utilities shut off illegally, or experiencing harassment—you might want to call emergency hotlines: - **Legal Assistance Hotline:** 800‑555‑1234 (example number) - **Local Shelter/Tenant Advocacy Group:** Search online for “tenant advocacy near me.” Feel free to ask more detailed questions!
